chapter_theme: Friendship with one who is inwardly hostile: smiles, soft words, folded hands and even tears can hide a weapon. In the end the chapter tells the reader to answer such a person with the same outward show.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the defect of such friendship (821-822), why it is cruel (823-824), not to trust their words (825-827), not to trust their acts (828), and how to deal with them (829-830).

821.reading: The friendship of those who come close without inner consent is an anvil for striking, once they find the right place.
821.nuance: A பட்டடை seems to hold a thing up and in fact is what makes the blow cut, so Pope's gloss 'weapon' loses the image. The false friend need not be the blade. The support he gives is what enables it.

822.reading: The friendship of those who seem one's own but aren't will change the way women's minds change.
822.nuance: The verse itself makes a general comparison about women, and the commentators' responses show how uneasy it is.

positions.position: Women's minds are changeable once there is an opportunity, and he supports it from another text.
positions.quote: இடம் பெற்றால் பெண்பாலார் மனம் போல வேறுபடும்.

positions.position: The comparison concerns only prostitutes, who pretend to the virtue that women have, so women in general are not the target.

823.reading: Though they have studied many good things, it is hard for the unworthy to become good at heart.
823.nuance: The verse separates learning from moral change. This limit matters to a text that elsewhere praises study so highly.

positions.position: மாணார் are enemies, and learning won't make them friends, so don't trust them because they are learned.
positions.quote: அதனான் மனம் திருந்தி நட்பாதல் பகைவர்க்கு இல்லை

positions.position: மாணார் are simply those lacking excellence, and the point is about what learning can reveal.

824.reading: Fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while within they are bitter.
824.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives the reason for fear: the face is the instrument for reading intentions, and here the malice doesn't show on it.

825.reading: Those not in accord with you in mind are not to be trusted on the strength of their words in anything.
825.nuance: The verse states no authority, but Parimelazhagar supplies one: 'the treatises on policy' say so. He reads the line as counsel on whom to trust in practical affairs (கருமங்கள்).

826.reading: Though they say good things as friends do, the words of the unreconciled are quickly seen through.
826.nuance: This verse is more optimistic than its neighbours about detection. Parimelazhagar reads the concession to mean they rarely say good things at all.

827.reading: Do not take humility in an enemy's speech as humility, for the bending of a bow means harm.
827.nuance: Parimelazhagar marks it as 'word-bowing' and not real bowing, since the man himself doesn't bow. The bend is what stores the force, so the humility may be the very preparation.

828.reading: A weapon hides even inside hands folded in worship, and an enemy's shed tears are the same.
828.nuance: The chapter moves from words to the body, and it picks the gestures hardest to doubt, reverence and grief. Parimelazhagar's line is that those able to read intent see the weapon even in the moment of reassurance.

829.reading: Those who overdo friendship and despise you inwardly should be made to smile, and embraced in friendship so that it dies.
829.nuance: The verse itself gives no audience, but Parimelazhagar supplies 'royal policy' and says plainly that having one thing inside and another outside is wrong in general but proper toward enemies. He treats it as a licensed exception. சாப்புல்லல் is a hard phrase: this reading follows the commentators, and Pope's couplet ('slap') goes elsewhere.

830.reading: When the time comes that an enemy turns friend, befriend with the face, let go in the heart, and then let it go altogether.
830.nuance: Parimelazhagar narrows the permission to a moment when open rejection isn't possible, and stresses a final exit. So the mask is a temporary means, not a settled way of life.

links.note: 706 says the face shows what is in the heart as crystal shows what is beside it. 824 fears those whose face shows the reverse. Chapter 71 rests on the reliability of signs and chapter 83 on their failure, and Parimelazhagar's note on 824 calls the face the instrument of reading.
824 fears hostility that does not show. 826 says an enemy's fine words are soon seen through. The chapter holds two views on whether concealment can succeed.

279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is kind, so judge by deed. 827 says the bent bow means harm. The two verses reach for the same geometry to make the same point, that shape doesn't reveal intent.
71 says love can't be locked in, and that tears publish it. 828 says an enemy's tears may hide a weapon. The evidence that the Book of Virtue trusts absolutely is, in the Book of Wealth, a cover.

34 says all virtue comes to a stainless mind and the rest is noise. 829 teaches outward friendship with inward death. Parimelazhagar accepts the conflict openly and resolves it as a rule for enemies only, which is a substantive claim about how the books of the Kural relate.
786 says friendship of the face alone is not friendship. 830 tells the reader to use just that kind on a suspect enemy (முகம் நட்டு). What is a failure in one chapter becomes a technique in another.

source_issues: 822: Parimelazhagar's text starts with a verse fragment and a stray HTML piece (br>).
825, 827, 828, 830: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption (தௌ¢, வௌ¢).
829: Manakkudavar's text is marked [#] and is nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's word-gloss, so it may not be independent; not used as a separate voice.
